headline: A doubling find-rate that mostly measures who didn't file
summary: This month's stop-and-search data shows the recorded national find rate jumping from 27.8% in February to 51.5% in April (2026-04), while monthly totals fell from 37,688 to 29,588. Before anyone concludes searches suddenly got twice as accurate, note that 14 forces — including the Metropolitan Police, the single largest by volume — are missing from the latest month. The steadier picture is the rolling 12-month window of 461,540 searches, in which drugs remain the dominant stated object and 'no further action' the dominant outcome. The city crime figures are useful for composition but riddled with reporting gaps and snapped-location quirks, so we read them cautiously.

items.title: The find-rate 'leap' is an artefact of who's reporting, not better targeting
items.body: The recorded find rate sits around 0.29 for most of the year, then jumps to 0.507 in March and 0.515 in April — almost doubling. Over the same two months the monthly total drops from 37,688 (Feb) to 29,690 (Mar) to 29,588 (Apr). That coincides with 14 forces missing the latest month, including the Metropolitan Police, whose 12-month volume of 118,649 dwarfs every other force. When high-volume forces drop out, both the count and the find rate can swing sharply. Treat the jump as a composition effect, not a real change in search effectiveness.

items.title: The 12-month window is the figure to lean on: 461,540 searches
items.body: Across the rolling year, 461,540 searches were recorded. The single most common stated object was controlled drugs at 245,734 — about 53% — followed by 'not stated' (67,779), offensive weapons (52,129) and stolen goods (47,048). The large 'not stated' category is itself worth noting: nearly one in seven records doesn't specify what was being looked for, which limits how cleanly you can describe what searches are actually for.

items.title: Most searches end in no further action
items.body: In the 12-month window, 290,231 outcomes — roughly 63% — were 'a no further action disposal'. Arrests accounted for 67,867 (about 15%), community resolutions 47,022, and 42,012 outcomes were 'not stated'. This is the steadier counterpart to the volatile monthly find rate, and it shows that the majority of recorded searches do not lead to a formal sanction. That is a description of recorded outcomes, not a verdict on whether any individual search was justified.

items.title: Ethnicity shares are recorded here — but they cannot answer the disproportionality question
items.body: The window records 280,518 searches of people logged as White (about 61%), 74,998 Black (16%), 51,093 Asian (11%), with 36,427 'not stated'. These are raw counts only. There is no population denominator in this dataset, so it is impossible to say any group is 'over-' or 'under-searched' from these figures alone. To judge disproportionality you would need local resident or street-population baselines, which are not supplied here.

items.title: Some force-level find rates are too tidy to take at face value
items.body: Among forces that did report the latest month, Thames Valley shows a find rate of 1.0 (100%) and West Yorkshire 0.918 — figures that almost certainly reflect partial filing, where only resolved or successful searches have been uploaded so far, rather than genuinely near-perfect targeting. Note too that Lancashire records 7,041 searches in the latest month against a 12-month total of 29,094 — far above its monthly average — with no find rate at all. These are reasons to wait for fuller data before ranking forces.

items.title: City crime counts: read the composition, mind the gaps
items.body: London's latest month shows 4,487 recorded crimes, led by theft from the person (1,035) and other theft (875) — a central-London profile, since the city point is a busy snapped location, not the whole capital. By contrast Manchester shows just 4 crimes, an obvious reporting gap rather than a safe city. Several series have visible dips that look like filing artefacts — Newcastle fell to 456 in January 2026 between months above 800 — so month-to-month wobbles should not be read as real swings in offending.

caveats: The latest month (2026-04) is incomplete: 14 forces, including the Metropolitan Police, West Midlands and Greater Manchester, are missing. The rolling 12-month window is the more reliable basis for any comparison.
All figures are recorded counts. 'Rose' or 'fell' describes the data as filed, not the underlying level of crime or searching, and none of these numbers can establish cause and effect.
Stop-and-search ethnicity figures are raw shares with no population denominator, so they cannot show disproportionality in either direction.

Crime locations are anonymised and snapped to representative points; a 'city' point reflects a central area, not the whole urban area, and very low counts (e.g. Manchester's 4) usually signal missing data.
Find rates and totals can shift simply because a large force files late or early; large month-to-month moves here are more likely reporting effects than real change.
